Where it began

Abhimanyu Mithun was born in Bengaluru on 25 October 1989. Cricket was not his first sport. As a teenager he threw the javelin at state level and spent long hours in his father's gym, but the discus refused to go where he wanted it to, and a friend talked him into trying a cricket camp instead.

He had not bowled with a leather ball until he was 17. It did not take him long to make up for lost time.

The player

He was a right-arm fast-medium bowler who played his first-class cricket for Karnataka, and he arrived in a rush. On his first-class debut he took six wickets in the first innings and five in the second, a hat-trick among them. That 2009–10 Ranji Trophy season he finished with 47 wickets, more than anyone else, and he was called into the India squad for a Test against South Africa barely ten weeks after that first game.

His Test debut came against Sri Lanka at Galle in July 2010, and he took four wickets. He played 4 Tests between 2010 and 2011, taking 9 wickets with a best of 4 for 105, and he also played one-day internationals for India.

What made him special

Pace, above all. His Karnataka coach spoke of a bowler who ran in at around 140 km/h and did well at every level he played. He kept producing for Karnataka long after his Test days, too. In October 2019 he took a hat-trick in the final of the Vijay Hazare Trophy, which Karnataka went on to win, and the next month he took five wickets in a single over, hat-trick included, in a Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy semi-final. No bowler before him had managed a hat-trick in each of India's three top domestic formats.

He was a handier batsman than most fast bowlers. At Galle he went in at number 11, looked sturdier than the men around him, and was moved up to number 9 for the second innings, where he made 25. His Test runs came at 24.00, with a best of 46, a batting average plenty of specialist bowlers would envy.

Away from the middle

In the IPL he turned out for Royal Challengers Bangalore and later Mumbai Indians, who picked him for his bowling at the end of an innings. He also played for India Red in the Duleep Trophy. He retired from all forms of the game in October 2021.

And finally

Not many fast bowlers learned the game after their 17th birthday, and fewer again took a hat-trick in every format at home. For a man who started with a javelin, he found the right thing to throw in the end.
